name: React
description: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from small reusable components.

blocks.html:
Introduction & JSX

What is React?

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Instead of writing one huge page, you build many small pieces called components, such as a button, a menu or a product card. You then put the pieces together like building blocks. When your data changes, React updates only the parts of the page that need to change.

React is a library, not a full framework. It focuses on the user interface. For other things, such as routing or fetching data, you add other tools. Today React code is written with function components and hooks. (Older code used class components, but you do not need them for new projects.)

Create a project with Vite

The fastest way to start is Vite, a build tool that gives you a quick dev server. You need Node.js installed first. Then run these commands in a terminal:

npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev

The last command starts a local server, usually at http://localhost:5173. Open it in the browser and you will see the starter page. Edit src/App.jsx and save: the page updates at once. The important files are:

FilePurpose
index.htmlThe single HTML page. It has an empty div id="root".
src/main.jsxStarts React and draws your App inside the root div.
src/App.jsxYour first component. You will edit this most.
package.jsonLists your dependencies and scripts like dev and build.

Your first component with JSX

A component is a JavaScript function that returns what should appear on screen. The tag-like code it returns is called JSX. JSX looks like HTML, but it is really JavaScript. Your build tool turns it into normal JavaScript calls before the browser runs it.

blocks.output: Browser shows: a large heading that says "Hello, React!"

blocks.html:
Expressions in curly braces

Inside JSX you can use any JavaScript expression by putting it in curly braces. An expression is anything that produces a value: a variable, a calculation, or a function call. Statements such as if or for do not work inside the braces.

blocks.output: Browser shows: Welcome, Ali. Next year is 2027.

blocks.html:
JSX rules

JSX is a little stricter than HTML. Learn these rules and most beginner errors disappear.

  • A component must return one parent element. If you do not want an extra div, wrap the pieces in a fragment: <>...</>.
  • Close every tag, even empty ones: write <br /> and <input />.
  • Use className instead of class, because class is a reserved word in JavaScript.
  • Attribute names use camelCase, for example onClick and tabIndex.
  • The style attribute takes an object, so you write two pairs of braces: one pair for JavaScript and one pair for the object.
  • Component names start with a capital letter. Lowercase names like div are normal HTML tags.

blocks.output: Browser shows: a heading "Learning Hub" and, below it, a paragraph "Styled text" in teal colour.

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Writing class="box" instead of className="box".
  • Returning two sibling elements without a parent or fragment.
  • Forgetting to close a tag such as <img> or <input>.
  • Naming a component in lowercase, so React treats it as an HTML tag.

Key Points

  • React builds user interfaces from small reusable components.
  • Use npm create vite@latest to start a project and npm run dev to run it.
  • A function component returns JSX, which looks like HTML but is JavaScript.
  • Put JavaScript expressions inside curly braces.
  • Use className, close all tags, and return a single parent or a fragment.

Components & Props

Function components

A React component is a plain JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX. Once you have defined a component, you use it like an HTML tag. Components let you write a piece of the page once and reuse it many times. (Long ago React also had class components, but modern code uses function components only.)

It is a good habit to put each component in its own file, for example src/Greeting.jsx, and export it with export default. Then you import it where you need it.

Props: giving data to a component

Props (short for properties) are the inputs of a component. The parent writes them like HTML attributes, and the child receives them as one object. Most people use destructuring in the parameter list to pick out the props they need.

Props flow in one direction: from parent down to child. A child must treat its props as read-only and never change them. If a value must change over time, you use state, which you will learn in the next lesson.

blocks.output:
Browser shows two paragraphs:
Hello, Sara!
Hello, Bilal!

blocks.html:
Default values and non-string props

A string prop can use quotes, like name="Sara". For numbers, booleans, arrays or variables, use curly braces: amount={500}. You can give a prop a default value in the destructuring, so it works even when the parent leaves it out.

blocks.output: Browser shows: PKR 500 and USD 20

blocks.html:
Children and composition

Whatever you put between the opening and closing tags of a component arrives as a special prop called children. This lets you build wrapper components, such as a card, a layout or a modal, that can hold anything. Building big components out of smaller ones is called composition, and it is the main way to reuse code in React.

blocks.output: Browser shows: a card box with the heading "Course" and below it the paragraph "React Basics".

blocks.html:
Remember

IdeaExample
String prop<Greeting name="Sara" />
Number or variable prop<Price amount={500} />
Default valuefunction Price({ currency = "PKR" })
Children<Card>...</Card> and {children}

Common mistakes: forgetting the curly braces around a number (you then pass the string "500"), writing a component name in lowercase, and trying to change a prop inside the child.

Key Points

  • A component is a function with a capital first letter that returns JSX.
  • Props are inputs. They flow from parent to child and are read-only.
  • Destructure props in the parameter list and give defaults with =.
  • Use children to build wrapper components.
  • Build large screens by composing small components.

State & Events

Why we need state

A normal variable inside a component is forgotten every time the component runs again, and changing it does not update the screen. State solves both problems. State is data that a component remembers between renders. When state changes, React runs the component again (a re-render) and shows the new result on the screen.

useState and onClick

You create state with the useState hook. It takes the starting value and gives back a pair: the current value and a function to change it. We use array destructuring to name them, like const [count, setCount] = useState(0).

To respond to the user, you add an event handler such as onClick. Pass a function, not the result of calling a function. Write onClick={handleClick} or onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}. Do not write onClick={handleClick()}, because that runs the function while the page is drawing.

blocks.output:
Button shows: Clicked 0 times
After three clicks the button shows: Clicked 3 times

blocks.html:
Do not mutate state

Never change a state value directly, for example count = count + 1 or items.push("x"). React only notices a change when you call the setter with a new value. For numbers and strings this is easy. For arrays and objects, make a copy with the spread syntax and change the copy.

blocks.output:
Paragraph shows: Read
After one click on Add: Read, Write
After two clicks: Read, Write, Write

blocks.html:
Updating from the previous value

The state value you see inside a render is a snapshot. If you call setCount(count + 1) three times in one handler, all three calls use the same old count, so the result is only +1. When the new value depends on the old one, pass an updater function: setCount(c => c + 1). React applies the updates one after another.

blocks.output:
Button shows: Count: 0
After one click the button shows: Count: 3

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Calling the handler in JSX: onClick={add()} instead of onClick={add}.
  • Changing an array or object in place instead of making a new copy.
  • Expecting the variable to change right after calling the setter. The new value appears on the next render.
  • Calling useState inside an if statement or a loop. Hooks must be called at the top level of the component.

Key Points

  • State is memory that a component keeps between renders.
  • useState(initial) returns [value, setValue].
  • Changing state with the setter causes a re-render.
  • Pass a function to onClick; do not call it.
  • Never mutate state. Create a new array or object instead.
  • Use setX(x => ...) when the new value depends on the old one.

Lists, Keys & Conditional Rendering

Rendering a list with map

Real apps show lists: courses, messages, products. In React you do not write a loop in the JSX. You use the array method map to turn each data item into a JSX element. The result is an array of elements, and React displays them all.

Every item in a list needs a key prop. React uses keys to match each element with its data when the list changes, so it can add, remove or move items correctly and quickly.

blocks.output:
Browser shows a bulleted list:
- Mango
- Apple
- Guava

blocks.html:
Choosing good keys

A key must be unique among siblings and stable, meaning the same item always has the same key. The best key is an id from your data, such as a database id. Avoid using the array index as the key when the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted, because the keys then point to different data and you can get strange bugs. The key is used by React only; it is not passed to your component as a prop.

blocks.output:
Browser shows a bulleted list:
- HTML (done)
- CSS (pending)
- React (pending)

blocks.html:
Conditional rendering

You often need to show something only in some cases. JSX has no special syntax for this. You use normal JavaScript:

  • Ternary: cond ? <A /> : <B /> chooses one of two options.
  • Logical AND: cond && <A /> shows A only when cond is true.
  • Early return: if (!user) return null; stops the component and shows nothing.

Be careful with && and numbers. If count is 0, then count && <p>..</p> shows the number 0 on the page. Use a real comparison such as count > 0 && ....

blocks.output:
Browser shows: the heading "Inbox" and the paragraph "You have 3 new messages."
(With count={0} only the heading would appear.)

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

MistakeFix
No key on list items (React warns in the console)Add key={item.id} to the outer element inside map.
Using the index as key in a list that changes orderUse a stable id from the data.
Putting the key on an inner elementThe key goes on the element returned directly by map.
count && ... shows 0Use count > 0 && ... or a ternary.

Key Points

  • Use array.map() to turn data into JSX elements.
  • Give each list item a unique, stable key, preferably an id.
  • Use a ternary for either/or, and && for show-or-nothing.
  • An early return can skip rendering completely.

Forms & Controlled Inputs

Controlled inputs

In plain HTML, an input keeps its own text. In React, the usual way is a controlled input: the text lives in React state, and the input just displays it. You give the input a value from state and an onChange handler that updates the state with what the user typed. The state is then the single source of truth.

The handler receives an event object. The text typed by the user is in e.target.value.

blocks.output:
Browser shows: an empty input with the hint "Your name" and the paragraph "Hello,"
After typing Sara in the input the paragraph shows: Hello, Sara

blocks.html:
Submitting a form

Use a form element with an onSubmit handler. By default the browser reloads the page when a form is submitted. Call e.preventDefault() at the start of your handler to stop that, then do your own work with the state values. A button with type="submit" inside the form, or pressing Enter, triggers the submit event.

blocks.output:
After typing sara@example.com and clicking Subscribe, the paragraph shows: Subscribed: sara@example.com
The page does not reload.

blocks.html:
Many fields, one state object

For bigger forms you do not need one state variable per field. Keep one object, give each input a name that matches a key, and use one shared handler. The syntax [e.target.name]: e.target.value uses a computed key, so the handler updates whichever field changed. Remember to copy the old object with ...form so the other fields stay.

blocks.output:
At first the paragraph shows: from Lahore
After typing Sara and choosing Karachi it shows: Sara from Karachi

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Setting value without onChange. The input becomes read-only and React warns you.
  • Forgetting e.preventDefault(), so the page reloads and the state is lost.
  • Forgetting ...form when updating an object, which erases the other fields.
  • Using useState() with no start value for a text input. Start with an empty string "".
  • Checkboxes use checked and e.target.checked, not value.

Key Points

  • A controlled input gets value from state and updates it in onChange.
  • Read the typed text with e.target.value.
  • Use onSubmit on the form and call e.preventDefault().
  • For many fields, keep one object in state and use the input name.

useEffect & Fetching Data

What is an effect?

Rendering a component should only calculate JSX. But apps also need to do work that reaches outside React: fetch data from a server, start a timer, or change the page title. This kind of work is called a side effect, and you put it inside the useEffect hook.

Timing: React first renders your component and updates the screen. After that, it runs your effect. So an effect never blocks the first paint.

The dependency array

The second argument of useEffect is the dependency array. It tells React when to run the effect again.

CodeWhen the effect runs
useEffect(fn)After every render
useEffect(fn, [])Once, after the first render
useEffect(fn, [count])After the first render and whenever count changes

Put every state or prop that the effect uses into the array. In development, React StrictMode runs effects an extra time on mount on purpose, to help you find bugs. This does not happen in the production build.

blocks.output:
Console shows after the first render: Effect ran, count is 0
After one click: Effect ran, count is 1
(In development with StrictMode, the first line appears twice.)

blocks.html:
Cleanup

An effect can return a cleanup function. React calls it before the effect runs again and when the component is removed from the page. Use it to undo what the effect started: stop a timer, close a connection, or remove an event listener. Without cleanup you can get memory leaks and strange repeated behaviour.

blocks.output:
Browser shows: Seconds: 0
After one second: Seconds: 1
After two seconds: Seconds: 2 (and so on)

blocks.html:
Fetching data with loading and error states

A request takes time and can fail, so a good component tracks three things: the data, a loading flag, and an error. Show a loading message first, then either the error or the data. The effect below runs once, calls the server with fetch, and updates the state when the answer arrives.

blocks.output:
Browser first shows: Loading...
Then it shows a list of three names: Leanne Graham, Ervin Howell, Clementine Bauch
If the network fails it shows an Error message instead.

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Leaving out the dependency array, so the effect runs after every render. If it also sets state, this can make an endless loop.
  • Forgetting a value in the array, so the effect uses old data.
  • Making the effect function itself async. Call an async function inside it instead.
  • Not checking res.ok. A 404 response is not an error for fetch by itself.
  • Forgetting cleanup for timers and listeners.

Key Points

  • Effects run after React has updated the screen.
  • The dependency array controls when an effect runs again.
  • Return a cleanup function to stop timers and listeners.
  • For fetching, keep data, loading and error in state and show each case.

Sharing State

Lifting state up

Sometimes two components need the same data. For example, an input and a text that shows its length. Props only go down, so siblings cannot talk to each other directly. The solution is to lift the state up: move it to the closest parent that contains both components. The parent passes the value down as a prop and passes a function down so the child can ask for a change.

blocks.output:
Browser shows: an empty input and the paragraph "Length: 0"
After typing React the paragraph shows: Length: 5

blocks.html:
Context: avoiding prop drilling

If many levels of components sit between the owner of the data and the component that needs it, passing props through every level becomes tiring. This is called prop drilling. Context lets a parent make a value available to every component below it, however deep.

There are three steps: create the context with createContext, wrap part of the tree with a Provider that gives a value, and read the value with useContext in any child. Context is good for data used by many components, such as the theme, the logged-in user or the language. (In React 19 you can write the context itself as the provider, <ThemeContext value="dark">, but .Provider still works everywhere.)

blocks.output: Browser shows: Theme is dark

blocks.html:
A custom hook for shared state

A custom hook is a normal function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks. It lets you reuse logic. A common pattern is a provider component that owns the state, plus a small hook that reads the context. Components then simply call useTheme().

blocks.output:
Button shows: Theme: light
After one click the button shows: Theme: dark
After a second click it shows: Theme: light

blocks.html:
Which tool to use?

SituationChoose
Only one component needs the dataLocal useState
A parent and a few children need itLift the state up and pass props
Many distant components need itContext
You repeat the same hook logicA custom hook

Common mistakes: using context for everything (start with props), reading a context outside its Provider (you get the default value), and forgetting that all components using a context re-render when its value changes.

Key Points

  • Lift state up to the closest common parent when components must share it.
  • Context passes data to deep children without prop drilling.
  • Use createContext, a Provider with value, and useContext.
  • A custom hook is a function starting with use that reuses hook logic.
  • Start simple with props, and add context only when you need it.

Routing & Deployment

Routing with react-router

A React app is usually a single HTML page, but users expect different URLs such as /about or /courses/7. A router shows the right component for the current URL without reloading the page. The most popular choice is react-router. Install it with:

npm install react-router-dom

You wrap the app in BrowserRouter, list your pages inside Routes, and describe each page with a Route that has a path and an element. For links, use the Link component instead of the a tag, because Link changes the URL without a full page reload.

blocks.output:
At the address / the browser shows: Home | About and the heading "Home page"
After clicking About the address becomes /about and the heading is "About page". The page does not reload.

blocks.html:
URL parameters

A path can contain a part that changes, written with a colon, like /courses/:id. Inside the page component, the hook useParams gives you the value. This is how one component can show many different items.

blocks.output: When the address is /courses/7 the browser shows: Course number 7

blocks.html:
Environment variables

Apps often need settings that differ between your computer and the live site, such as the address of the API. Vite reads them from a file named .env in the project root. Only names that start with VITE_ are made available to your code, through import.meta.env. After you change the .env file, restart the dev server.

Warning: these values are copied into the JavaScript that users download. Never put passwords or secret keys in a VITE_ variable.

blocks.output: Browser shows: API: https://api.example.com

blocks.html:
Build and deploy to Vercel

The dev server is only for development. For the real site, create an optimised build:

npm run build
npm run preview

npm run build runs vite build and writes the final files into the dist folder. npm run preview lets you test that build locally. To publish it on Vercel:

  1. Push your project to a GitHub repository.
  2. Sign in to Vercel and import the repository.
  3. Vercel detects Vite. The build command is npm run build and the output folder is dist.
  4. Add your VITE_ variables in the project settings, then deploy.

Because the router handles URLs in the browser, a direct visit to /about must still load index.html. On Vercel, add a vercel.json file with a rewrite that sends all paths to /. Every new push to GitHub then deploys again automatically.

Common mistakes

  • Using <a href> for internal pages, which reloads the whole app. Use Link.
  • Naming a variable API_URL without the VITE_ prefix, so it is undefined in your code.
  • Putting secrets in VITE_ variables.
  • Getting a 404 on refresh after deploying, because the rewrite to index.html is missing.

Key Points

  • react-router shows a component per URL: BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link.
  • useParams reads parts of the URL such as :id.
  • Environment variables must start with VITE_ and are public.
  • npm run build creates the dist folder for deployment.
  • Vercel builds from your GitHub repository and needs a rewrite for client-side routes.
